fetched_contents.text: Comprehensive insights into herbicide resistance mechanisms in weeds: a synergistic integration of transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses Abstract Omics techniques, including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics have smoothed the researcher’s ability to generate hypotheses and discover various agronomically relevant functions and mechanisms, as well as their implications and associations. With a significant increase in the number of cases with resistance to multiple herbicide modes of action, studies on herbicide resistance are currently one of the predominant areas of research within the field of weed science. High-throughput technologies have already started revolutionizing the current molecular weed biology studies. The evolution of herbicide resistance in weeds (particularly via non-target site resistance mechanism) is a perfect example of a complex, multi-pathway integration-induced response. To date, functional genomics, including transcriptomic and metabolomic studies have been used separately in herbicide resistance research, however there is a substantial lack of integrated approach. Hence, despite the ability of omics technologies to provide significant insights into the molecular functioning of weeds, using a single omics can sometimes be misleading. This mini-review will aim to discuss the current progress of transcriptome-based and metabolome-based approaches in herbicide resistance research, along with their systematic integration. Keywords: abiotic stresses, herbicide resistance, metabolomics, omics technologies, transcriptomic regulation 1. Introduction Herbicide resistance among weeds has become a major reason for food security problems since the early years of synthetic herbicide development. Since then, there has been a continuous increase in the frequency of herbicide resistance cases, a major plant protection challenge encountered by farmers across the planet. Herbicides have been used to control weeds and increase the quality and quantity of major crops since their discovery. However, repeated use of similar herbicidal modes of action (MOAs) and the associated selection pressure have led to the evolution of herbicide resistance in varieties of economically important weedy species such as Alopecurus myosuroides (Lan et al., 2022; Goldberg-Cavalleri et al., 2023), Amaranthus palmeri (Manicardi et al., 2023), Apera spica venti (Košnarová et al., 2021; Papapanagiotou et al., 2022), Bromus sterilis (Sen et al., 2021), Lolium spp (Tehranchian et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2023). Recent studies showed that the majority of these weeds were also developing multiple resistances against herbicides with more than one mode of action (Tehranchian et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2020; Košnarová et al., 2021; Lan et al., 2022; Papapanagiotou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). From a molecular point of view, herbicide resistance mechanisms might be categorized into target-site based resistance (TSR) and non-target-site based resistance (NTSR) (Torra and Alcántara-de la Cruz, 2022). Briefly, TSR comprises single or multiple nucleotide polymorphisms (point mutations), codon deletion (till date there is only one evidence in the case of protoporphyrinogen oxidase in Amaranthus sp.) and target gene overexpression (either via transcriptional regulatory mechanisms or via gene amplification) (Gaines et al., 2020). On the other hand, NTSR constitutes enhanced metabolism [via cytochrome P450s (Cyp450s), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs) and glycosyltransferases (GTs)], reduced uptake and translocation, vacuolar sequestration and increased ability to deal with oxygen radicals (Gaines et al., 2020). More details on these mechanisms can be found in Gaines et al., 2020. Reports show that the NTSR is more complicated and trickier to understand than the TSR (Jugulam and Shyam, 2019). Nevertheless, irrespective of the specific resistance mechanism, herbicide-resistant weeds, if left uncontrolled, will pose a significant threat to the global agricultural sector. High-throughput molecular technologies (such as genomics, proteomics, metabolomics, transcriptomics etc.) have the potential to offer great analytical opportunities to understand and identify the mechanisms of herbicide resistance, thus leading to the identification of novel herbicidal MOAs (Ravet et al., 2018). Development of herbicide resistance in weeds is similar to that of abiotic stress resistance development in plants and can provide insights into the stress resistance mechanisms in plants in general (Hamouzová et al., 2023). Even though during the last decade, continuous progress has been made in the field of DNA, RNA, and protein-based omics studies in herbicide resistance, substantial research areas are yet to be explored. Additionally, to our knowledge, inadequate initiatives have been taken to integrate multiple omics-based studies to elucidate the mechanisms of herbicide resistance in economically significant weeds. Hence, in this mini-review, we will confine our discussion to transcriptomics, metabolomics and the need for their systematic integration to unravel the molecular mechanisms of herbicide resistance in weeds. The transcriptome and metabolome represent two key layers of biological information that can provide novel insights into how weeds develop resistance against herbicides. While transcriptomics provides a global overview on the expression profile of the genes, metabolomics provides a global overview on metabolic pathways and their regulation (Maroli et al., 2018a). 2. fetched_contents.text: Management of Infection by Parasitic Weeds: A Review Abstract Parasitic plants rely on neighboring host plants to complete their life cycle, forming vascular connections through which they withdraw needed nutritive resources. In natural ecosystems, parasitic plants form one component of the plant community and parasitism contributes to overall community balance. In contrast, when parasitic plants become established in low biodiversified agroecosystems, their persistence causes tremendous yield losses rendering agricultural lands uncultivable. The control of parasitic weeds is challenging because there are few sources of crop resistance and it is difficult to apply controlling methods selective enough to kill the weeds without damaging the crop to which they are physically and biochemically attached. The management of parasitic weeds is also hindered by their high fecundity, dispersal efficiency, persistent seedbank, and rapid responses to changes in agricultural practices, which allow them to adapt to new hosts and manifest increased aggressiveness against new resistant cultivars. New understanding of the physiological and molecular mechanisms behind the processes of germination and haustorium development, and behind the crop resistant response, in addition to the discovery of new targets for herbicides and bioherbicides will guide researchers on the design of modern agricultural strategies for more effective, durable, and health compatible parasitic weed control. Keywords: Orobanche, Phelipanche, Striga, Cuscuta, germination, haustorium, crop resistance, bioherbicides, virulence, sustainable control 1. Introduction Approximately 1% of all angiosperms are parasitic on other plants and these plants are distributed among 28 dicotyledonous families having evolved the parasitic lifestyle independently at least 12 times [1,2,3,4,5]. Some are facultative parasites, capable of living autotrophically until reproduction, but shifting to a parasitic life form when a host is available to obtain nutrients with less investment in assimilation system. In comparison, obligated parasitic plants require the infection of another plant to survive shortly after germination. Parasitic plants can be also grouped by their photosynthesis competency, being either photosynthetically active hemiparasites or achlorophyllous holoparasites; or separated based upon the type of vascular connections they form with their host, being either xylem feeders or phloem feeders. They can also be grouped by the host plant organ to which they attach, either root feeders or shoot feeders [4,6]. While many parasitic plants have remained part of larger ecological communities, a small number of species have evolved to weediness, becoming troublesome pests in the agricultural field and an important constraint to crop productivity. Besides colonizing agroecosystems, parasitic plants are also present in urban ecosystems (Figure 1). While all agricultural weeds compete with crops for the space to obtain water, nutrients, and light, parasitic weeds are particularly noxious since they also directly extract valuable water and nutrients from the host plant. To extract nutrients from the host plants, parasitic weeds have evolved a unique multicellular structure termed the haustorium that invades the host, forms connections with the host vascular system, and withdraws its needed water and nutrients [7,8]. Successful haustorial connection to the host results in permanent damage during a large part of the crop life cycle, decreasing the crop value by reducing the harvested yield and contaminating it with parasitic seeds. Worldwide expansion of these noxious plant pests including the widely recognized genera Striga, Orobanche/Phelipanche, and Cuscuta has become a threat to food security [9]. There are few sources of crop resistance to parasitic plant infection [10,11]. The identified forms of resistance are classified as pre-attachment or post-attachment resistance according to whether the resistance occurs before or after the haustorium attaches the host surface [10]. Once the crop is infected, it is difficult to fend off the exhaustion of nutrients created by the attached parasite. Then, chemical control is the most frequent commercial method, albeit its application needs to observe specific recommendations for each parasitic life form [12]. In this review, we describe the current state of knowledge on the mechanisms controlling the infection process of parasitic weeds, and the defense systems and protection strategies employed by their hosts. 2. Infection by Parasitic Weeds All forms of parasitic weeds, facultative or obligate parasites, hemiparasites or holoparasites, root parasites, or stem parasites interact with the host crop by means of the haustorium [7]. Two main types of haustoria exist in root parasitic plants [1,8]. The terminal haustorium is typically developed by obligated parasitic weeds at the tip of their embryonic radicle. The lateral haustorium is developed as an extension in hemiparasitic radicle and mature roots of hemiparasitic and holoparasitic weeds. In aboveground parasitic weeds that infect crop stems and leaves, lateral haustoria develop as lateral extensions of their parasitic stems (Figure 2). The formation of a mature haustorium involves four developmental stages: Haustorium initiation, host invasion, establishment of host-parasite vascular continuity, and the creation of a parasitic sink that will be accepted by the crop as one of its own. Several mechanisms of crop location adapt the timing of haustorium development to the resource availability of its hosts [13]. 2.1. fetched_contents.text: Environmental Implication of Herbicide Use Abstract One of the guiding principles of the sustainable use of herbicides is their targeted action exclusively against weeds, consisting of blocking photosynthesis and synthesis of amino acids and growth regulators. Herbicides are major elements of plant production, indispensable to the functioning of modern agriculture. Nevertheless, their influence on all elements of the natural environment needs to be continuously controlled. This review article summarizes research addressing the effects of herbicides on the natural environment and the changes they trigger therein. Herbicides, applied to protect crops against weed infestation, are usually mixtures of various active substances; hence, it is generally difficult to analyze their impact on the environment and organisms. Nonetheless, an attempt was made in this review to discuss the effects of selected herbicides on individual elements of the natural environment (water, soil, and air) and organisms (humans, animals, plants, and microorganisms). In addition, the article presents examples of the biodegradation of selected herbicides and mechanisms of their degradation by bacteria and fungi. Based on this information, it can be concluded that the uncontrolled use of herbicides has led to adverse effects on non-target organisms, as documented in the scientific literature. However, further research on the environmental effects of these chemicals is needed address the missing knowledge on this subject. Keywords: herbicides, contamination, environmental, toxicity, organisms, biodegradation 1. Introduction Herbicides represent a group of chemical substances extensively applied to protect crops from weeds in order to improve their yield quality and quantity [1]. Their use has been reported as early as in Greek and Roman times. Democritus was the first to describe a herbicide, i.e., lupine flowers soaked in hemlock juice. Highly saline water was also used to kill weeds. One of the first herbicides was a by–product of olive oil production called amurca, the use of which was described in the manuals of Cato the Elder in around 150 BC. The first effective chemical herbicide was 6% copper sulfate, used in the 1940s for selective control of mustard in cereal stands. In turn, the first commercial inorganic herbicide was sodium arsenate, and the first organic herbicide was sodium dinitrocresylate developed in 1896 in France [2,3]. Despite advantages stemming from herbicide use, the use of chemicals in agriculture has led to slow changes in many ecosystems. Most of these chemical compounds penetrate into the soil, a process which is severely hazardous to the natural environment. Their accumulation in the soil impedes plant production, diminishes food safety and, consequently, poses risk to human health [4]. Jara and Winter [5] have reported that only 1% of pesticides reach their targets, while their remaining part pervades the soil and undergoes multiple conversions. Their residues in the soil and their metabolites migrate to other ecosystems, most often to the atmospheric air, underground and surface waters, and bottom deposits. These chemicals may cause the loss of biodiversity in various ecosystems and accumulate in different organisms [6,7,8,9]. The occurrence and migration of herbicides in the environment is a matter of concern; hence, all of the factors contributing to the hazard posed to ecosystems and organisms exposed to herbicides should be considered during their registration [10]. Investigations addressing the behavior of herbicides in the natural environment enable a complete understanding of the dynamics of their migration across the environment, including in particular their retention, transport and conversion, which are strongly intertwined and usually affect one another. The behavior and migration of herbicides across the environment depend on the chemical composition of their active substances, the matrix and environmental conditions. Effective control of weed infestation in crop stands is feasible upon thorough understanding of the fate of herbicides in the environment, and especially the mechanisms of their interaction with the environment [11]. Physicochemical properties of herbicides are one of the key factors affecting their initial distribution and behavior in the environment. Thus, the behavior of herbicides from the same chemical group will be similar in a given environment. Their main physicochemical properties determining initial behavior in the environment include acid-base dissociation constant (pKa/pKb), solubility in water (Sw), octanol–water partition coefficient (Kow), water vapor pressure (VP), sorption coefficient (Kd and Koc), half-life (DT50), and residual life in plants (RL50). These factors are particularly important in the case of pre-emergence herbicides applied at the onset of the growing season when both temperature and microbiological activity are relatively low [11,12,13,14]. During the application of herbicides, most of their active substances penetrate into the soil. Therefore, a perfect herbicide should have a half-life of less than 90 days, lipophilicity of logP < 2, and a recommended active substance dose below 200 g per 1 ha. The half-life of its active substance should not be too long, given the fact that it could cause potential contamination of underground waters, or problems associated with selectivity in successive crops. Therefore, in order for this active substance to migrate properly in the soil, it must have adequate solubility in water and mobility in the environment [14]. Taking into account all the above premises, this review article aimed to present (i) the effect of herbicides on the functioning of aquatic, soil and air ecosystems; (ii) migration of herbicides across the environment; (iii) outcomes of herbicide effects on organisms, i.e., humans, animals, plants, and microorganisms; and (iv) the potential of microorganisms for herbicide conversion…

Operational and agronomic limitations in legumes

Herbicide-treated crops for parasitic weed management in legumes face substantial agronomic challenges tied to crop physiology, weed competition, application windows, and effectiveness across diverse parasitic weed species. Legumes are particularly constrained by their physiology and the biology of parasitic weeds, which are described as “parasitic plants that rely on neighboring host plants to complete their life cycle” and “directly extract valuable water and nutrients from the host plant” [N4-F2]. The same source notes that parasitic weeds are especially noxious because they form vascular connections with the host and withdraw nutrients, and that parasitic weeds such as Striga, Orobanche/Phelipanche, and Cuscuta are now threatening food security [N4-F2]. This means parasitic weeds are not merely competitive; they are physiological parasites that attach, establish vascular links, and persist throughout the crop’s life cycle, making them harder to suppress with herbicides than ordinary weeds [N4-F2].

A key agronomic limitation is the timing of herbicide application and crop safety. The evidence states that parasitic weed control by introducing resistance to commercial herbicides into crop plants is a current strategy, but it also emphasizes that controlling parasitic weeds is challenging because it is difficult to apply methods selective enough to kill the weeds without damaging the crop to which they are physically and biochemically attached [N4-F2]. This directly supports a concern about herbicide application windows and crop safety: if the herbicide is applied too early, it may not reach the parasitic weed; if it is applied too late, the weed may already have established a vascular connection and become difficult to kill. The cited review also notes that parasitic weeds are often difficult to control with mechanical weeding and herbicide application, and that the same herbicide can vary in efficacy depending on the parasitic weed species [N4-R3]. That variation undermines a single uniform application window for all legume crops and parasitic weeds.

Crop physiology and weed competition dynamics are especially important in legumes because parasitic weeds attach to the host and extract resources, reducing the crop’s value and contaminating it with parasitic seeds [N4-F2]. The evidence further explains that parasitic weeds can become established in low-biodiversity agroecosystems, persisting and causing tremendous yield losses that can render agricultural lands uncultivable [N4-F2]. Legumes, which are often grown in systems where soil fertility and crop diversity are already constrained, face a double burden: not only must they compete with parasitic weeds for nutrients, but the weeds also alter the crop’s physiology by directly withdrawing resources and weakening its productivity [N4-F2]. This makes legumes more vulnerable to parasitic weed pressure and less responsive to herbicides if the weeds are already deeply established.

Effectiveness against diverse parasitic weed species is another major limitation. The review states that parasitic weeds include root feeders, shoot feeders, and species such as Striga, Orobanche/Phelipanche, and Cuscuta, and that parasitic weed control is challenging because there are few sources of crop resistance and it is difficult to apply selective controlling methods [N4-F2]. The herbicide evidence also notes that the efficacy of each herbicide varies with the parasitic weed species [N4-R1]. This means that a herbicide that works well against one species may be ineffective against another, and that legume crops may need tailored herbicide programs rather than one-size-fits-all treatments. The same source highlights that parasitic weeds have high fecundity, dispersal efficiency, persistent seedbanks, and rapid responses to changes in agricultural practices, which allow them to adapt to new hosts and manifest increased aggressiveness against new resistant cultivars [N4-F2]. This adaptability reduces the long-term effectiveness of herbicide-treated crops against parasitic weeds in legumes.

In sum, operational limitations in legumes include physiological vulnerability to parasitic attachment, competition for nutrients and resources, narrow herbicide application windows, and the need to manage multiple parasitic weed species with variable herbicide responses. These constraints are supported by the evidence on parasitic weed biology, herbicide efficacy, and the difficulty of selecting methods that damage weeds without damaging the crop [N4-F2][N4-R3][N4-R1].

Socioeconomic and ecological limitations

Herbicide-treated crops for parasitic weed management in legumes face significant socioeconomic and ecological limitations, including cost, labor, farmer adoption barriers, environmental risks, non-target effects, and long-term sustainability and resistance management concerns. The evidence indicates that parasitic weeds are a major constraint on agricultural production and that current management methods are limited [N2-R4]. The same source notes that parasitic weeds are difficult to control with selective methods, and that parasitic weeds pose a tremendous threat to world agriculture and are “almost uncontrollable” in some contexts [N2-R5]. This suggests that reliance on herbicides may be only a partial solution, with persistent socioeconomic and ecological trade-offs.

Cost, labor, and farmer adoption barriers are central. The review on parasitic weed management states that the only methods currently available to farmers are resistant varieties and chemical control, although both have their limitations [N2-R4]. It also states that parasitic weeds are difficult to apply controlling methods selective enough to kill the weeds without damaging the crop, which implies that herbicide-based systems may require specialized application equipment, timing, and labor [N4-F2]. The evidence on herbicide use adds that herbicides are major elements of plant production and indispensable to modern agriculture, but their influence on the natural environment needs continuous control [N5-F3]. This implies that herbicide adoption may be expensive and labor-intensive, especially in smallholder or resource-constrained settings where farmers face limited access to inputs and mechanization.

Environmental risks and non-target effects are another major limitation. The herbicide environmental review reports that herbicides are usually mixtures of various active substances, making their environmental impact difficult to analyze, and that uncontrolled use has led to adverse effects on non-target organisms [N5-F3]. It also states that herbicides can leach into soil and water systems, cause widespread contamination, and may accumulate in ecosystems, diminishing food safety and posing risks to human health [N5-F3]. The same source notes that herbicides may affect aquatic, soil, and air ecosystems, and that their migration across the environment depends on physicochemical properties such as solubility, partition coefficients, and half-life [N5-F3]. These points support the ecological concern that herbicide-treated crops for parasitic weed control may harm non-target plants, microbes, soil life, and water systems, which is especially problematic in legumes where the crop-weed relationship is already tightly integrated [N5-F3][N4-F2].

Long-term sustainability and resistance management are also critical. The herbicide resistance review explains that repeated use of similar herbicidal modes of action creates selection pressure and leads to the evolution of herbicide resistance in weeds [N1-F1]. It further states that multiple herbicide resistances are increasingly common, and that NTSR is more complicated and trickier to understand than TSR [N1-F1]. The parasitic weed evidence notes that parasitic weeds may develop herbicide resistance and that the use of herbicides may lead to the development of herbicide resistances [N6-R2]. This means that herbicide-treated crops with target-site resistance may not be a durable solution, because parasitic weeds can evolve resistance over time, and the same herbicide may become less effective as resistance spreads [N1-F1][N6-R2]. The parasitic weed review also highlights that parasitic weeds are highly fecund and can rapidly adapt to changes in agricultural practices, which increases the likelihood that new resistant cultivars will be attacked more aggressively [N4-F2].

In total, the socioeconomic and ecological limitations include high cost and labor demands, farmer adoption barriers, environmental contamination and non-target effects, and the risk of long-term resistance development. These constraints are supported by evidence on herbicide environmental impacts, parasitic weed control limitations, and herbicide resistance evolution [N5-F3][N2-R4][N1-F1][N6-R2].

Biological and genetic constraints of target-site resistance

Target-site resistance in crops and the potential for cross-resistance between herbicides and parasitic weeds are major biological and genetic constraints. The herbicide resistance review explains that resistance can develop through target-site resistance (TSR) or non-target-site resistance (NTSR), and that TSR typically involves point mutations, codon deletions, or target gene overexpression [N1-F1]. It also states that TSR generally affects herbicides with the same site of action, i.e., within the same herbicide group [N1-R5]. This mechanism is important because it means that crop resistance can be highly specific to one herbicide chemistry, which may not transfer directly to parasitic weeds.

Cross-resistance pathways between herbicides and parasitic weeds are not fully established in the provided evidence, but the evidence does point to the broader principle that herbicide resistance can evolve rapidly under repeated use and selection pressure. The review states that repeated use of similar herbicidal modes of action creates selection pressure and leads to the evolution of herbicide resistance in weeds [N1-F1]. It also notes that multiple herbicide resistances are becoming more common, and that NTSR is more complicated than TSR [N1-F1]. This suggests that parasitic weeds may develop resistance through herbicide exposure, but the evidence does not provide a direct pathway showing how parasitic weeds inherit target-site resistance from herbicide-treated crops or from crop resistance genes. Instead, the evidence supports a general concern that herbicides can drive resistance evolution in weeds and that parasitic weeds can evolve resistance to herbicides used against them [N6-R2].

Genetic and phenotypic stability of resistance traits is another constraint. The resistance review emphasizes that herbicide resistance mechanisms can be integrated and multi-pathway, and that transcriptomic and metabolomic studies are needed to understand these mechanisms more systematically [N1-F1]. It also notes that NTSR involves enhanced metabolism, reduced uptake and translocation, vacuolar sequestration, and increased ability to deal with oxygen radicals [N1-F1]. Because these resistance mechanisms are not limited to target-site changes, the genetic and phenotypic stability of resistance traits may vary. The review further states that NTSR is more complicated and trickier to understand than TSR, and that herbicide-resistant weeds pose a significant threat if left uncontrolled [N1-F1]. This implies that parasitic weed resistance may be unstable or context-dependent, and that resistance traits may not persist uniformly across species or environments.

In the context of parasitic weeds, the evidence also supports a concern that herbicides may lead to the development of herbicide resistance in parasitic weeds and that parasitic weed biology can complicate resistance management [N6-R2]. The parasitic weed review notes that parasitic weeds are highly fecund, have persistent seedbanks, and can rapidly respond to changes in agricultural practices, allowing them to adapt to new hosts and manifest increased aggressiveness against new resistant cultivars [N4-F2]. This suggests that parasitic weeds may not only inherit resistance through direct herbicide exposure but may also evolve more aggressive and persistent traits under selection pressure, making resistance management more difficult. The evidence also states that parasitic weeds are difficult to control with selective methods and that parasitic weed control by introducing resistance to commercial herbicides into crop plants is a current strategy [N4-F2].

Overall, the biological and genetic constraints of target-site resistance include specificity of TSR to herbicides in the same mode-of-action group, the potential for cross-resistance under repeated herbicide use, and the complexity of NTSR mechanisms. The provided evidence also supports the broader concern that parasitic weeds can develop herbicide resistance and that resistance traits may be unstable or difficult to manage in the long term [N1-F1][N6-R2][N4-F2].

Parasitic weed-specific resistance and management challenges

Parasitic weeds develop herbicide resistance through mechanisms that are closely tied to their biology and the agricultural environment. The evidence indicates that parasitic weeds are highly fecund, have persistent seedbanks, and respond rapidly to changes in agricultural practices, which allows them to adapt to new hosts and manifest increased aggressiveness against new resistant cultivars [N4-F2]. The herbicide resistance review also notes that repeated use of similar herbicidal modes of action creates selection pressure and leads to the evolution of herbicide resistance in weeds [N1-F1]. It further states that multiple herbicide resistances are increasingly common, and that non-target-site resistance is more complicated and trickier to understand than target-site resistance [N1-F1]. While the evidence does not provide a direct mechanistic pathway for parasitic weed resistance, it clearly supports the broader conclusion that parasitic weeds can evolve herbicide resistance under herbicide pressure.

Efficacy limits of herbicides against parasitic weeds are substantial. The parasitic weed review states that parasitic weed control is challenging because there are few sources of crop resistance and it is difficult to apply controlling methods selective enough to kill the weeds without damaging the crop [N4-F2]. It also notes that parasitic weeds are particularly noxious because they directly extract water and nutrients from the host plant, and that parasitic weeds such as Striga, Orobanche/Phelipanche, and Cuscuta are now threatening food security [N4-F2]. The herbicide evidence further reports that the efficacy of each herbicide varies with the parasitic weed species [N4-R1]. This means that herbicides may work well on some parasitic weed species but not others, limiting their usefulness as a universal parasitic weed management tool. The review also states that mechanical weeding and herbicide application are frequently ineffective when applied to parasitic weeds [N4-R3], reinforcing the idea that herbicides are not always sufficient on their own.

The interaction between crop resistance and weed biology is another important challenge. The parasitic weed review highlights that parasitic weeds are difficult to control because there are few sources of crop resistance [N4-F2]. It also notes that parasitic weeds form vascular connections with the host plant and withdraw nutrients, making them particularly damaging once they become established [N4-F2]. The evidence on herbicide-treated crops further states that parasitic weed control by introducing resistance to commercial herbicides into crop plants is a current strategy [N4-F2]. However, the same source emphasizes that controlling parasitic weeds is challenging because it is difficult to apply selective methods that do not damage the crop [N4-F2]. This creates a tension: crop resistance can help suppress parasitic weeds, but parasitic weeds can also evolve resistance to herbicides and adapt rapidly to new hosts and resistant cultivars [N4-F2][N6-R2]. The review also states that parasitic weeds are difficult to apply controlling methods selective enough to kill the weeds without damaging the crop to which they are physically and biochemically attached [N4-F2], indicating that even when herbicides are effective, they may still be hard to apply safely in legumes.

In addition, the evidence on parasitic weeds suggests that herbicides may not be sufficient to solve the problem on their own. The parasitic weed review notes that parasitic weeds are difficult to control with selective methods and that parasitic weeds pose a tremendous threat to world agriculture [N2-R5]. The herbicide resistance evidence adds that herbicide-resistant weeds pose a significant threat to the global agricultural sector if left uncontrolled [N1-F1]. Together, these points support the conclusion that parasitic weed-specific resistance and management challenges are not only about the weeds themselves but also about the ecological and genetic responses of parasitic weeds to herbicide selection pressure, host resistance, and changing agricultural practices [N4-F2][N1-F1][N6-R2].

# Integrated synthesis of challenges and limitations of herbicide-treated crops with target-site resistance for parasitic weeds in legumes

Herbicide-treated crops with target-site resistance are being considered as a tool to manage parasitic weeds in legumes, but the evidence shows that this approach faces a broad set of biological, operational, ecological, and socioeconomic limitations. The four branch reports consistently point to the same core conclusion: parasitic weeds are especially difficult to control because they are physiological parasites, have complex resistance pathways, and are highly responsive to changes in agricultural practice, while herbicide-treated crops may provide only partial or temporary relief.

## 1) Biological and genetic constraints of target-site resistance

A central challenge is that target-site resistance is not a universal solution. The evidence explains that resistance can develop through target-site resistance (TSR) or non-target-site resistance (NTSR), with TSR typically involving point mutations, codon deletions, or target gene overexpression [N1-F1]. It also notes that TSR generally affects herbicides with the same site of action, i.e., within the same herbicide group [N1-R5]. This means crop resistance can be highly specific, and it does not necessarily transfer directly to parasitic weeds.

The branch report on parasitic weed-specific resistance and management challenges adds that parasitic weeds may develop herbicide resistance under herbicide exposure and that repeated use of similar herbicidal modes of action can create selection pressure, leading to the evolution of herbicide resistance in weeds [N1-F1][N6-R2]. This is important because parasitic weeds can evolve resistance even when herbicides are used against them, which limits the durability of herbicide-treated crops with target-site resistance.

At the same time, the genetic and phenotypic stability of resistance traits is uncertain. The resistance review states that herbicide resistance mechanisms can be integrated and multi-pathway, and that transcriptomic and metabolomic studies are needed to understand them more systematically [N1-F1]. It also notes that NTSR involves enhanced metabolism, reduced uptake and translocation, vacuolar sequestration, and increased ability to deal with oxygen radicals [N1-F1]. Because these mechanisms are not limited to target-site changes, resistance traits may be context-dependent and difficult to stabilize. The parasitic weed evidence further emphasizes that parasitic weeds are highly fecund and can rapidly respond to changes in agricultural practices, allowing them to adapt to new hosts and manifest increased aggressiveness against new resistant cultivars [N4-F2]. This suggests that parasitic weed resistance may not only evolve through direct herbicide exposure but may also become more aggressive and persistent over time.

## 2) Operational and agronomic limitations in legumes

Legumes face particular agronomic challenges in parasitic weed management because parasitic weeds are not ordinary weeds. They are described as parasitic plants that rely on neighboring host plants to complete their life cycle and directly extract water and nutrients from the host plant [N4-F2]. This makes them especially damaging once they become established, because they form vascular connections with the host, weaken the crop, and reduce both yield and crop quality [N4-F2].

A major operational limitation is that parasitic weeds are difficult to control with selective methods that do not damage the crop to which they are physically and biochemically attached [N4-F2]. The same source states that parasitic weed control by introducing resistance to commercial herbicides into crop plants is a current strategy, but that controlling parasitic weeds is still challenging [N4-F2]. This implies that herbicide-treated crops may help, but they are not a complete solution. The herbicide evidence also reports that the efficacy of each herbicide varies with the parasitic weed species [N4-R1], meaning that a single herbicide may not work equally well against all parasitic weed species. This variability reduces the practical effectiveness of herbicide-treated crops in legumes.

Another agronomic constraint is herbicide application windows and crop safety. The parasitic weed review notes that parasitic weeds are difficult to apply controlling methods selective enough to kill the weeds without damaging the crop [N4-F2]. This supports the concern that herbicide application must be carefully timed, and that the crop’s physiology and weed competition dynamics make timing especially critical. The evidence also states that parasitic weeds are often difficult to control with mechanical weeding and herbicide application, and that parasitic weeds can persist and cause tremendous yield losses [N4-R3]. Together, these points show that herbicide-treated crops must be used within narrow application windows, and that crop safety remains a major concern.

Finally, effectiveness against diverse parasitic weed species is limited. Legumes are threatened by a range of parasitic weeds, including root feeders, shoot feeders, and species such as Striga, Orobanche/Phelipanche, and Cuscuta [N4-F2]. The review also states that parasitic weed control is challenging because there are few sources of crop resistance and it is difficult to apply selective controlling methods [N4-F2]. This means that herbicide-treated crops may need tailored programs for different parasitic weed species, rather than a single uniform treatment.

## 3) Parasitic weed-specific resistance and management challenges

Parasitic weeds develop herbicide resistance through biological and environmental pathways that are closely tied to their life history. The evidence shows that parasitic weeds are highly fecund, have persistent seedbanks, and respond rapidly to changes in agricultural practices, allowing them to adapt to new hosts and become more aggressive against new resistant cultivars [N4-F2]. This adaptability makes parasitic weed resistance difficult to manage, even when herbicides are used against them.

The branch report on parasitic weed-specific resistance also notes that herbicides may lead to the development of herbicide resistance in parasitic weeds [N6-R2]. Combined with the broader herbicide resistance review, this supports the conclusion that repeated herbicide use can drive resistance evolution in parasitic weeds, and that multiple herbicide resistances are increasingly common [N1-F1]. The review further states that non-target-site resistance is more complicated and trickier to understand than target-site resistance [N1-F1], which implies that parasitic weed resistance may involve multiple pathways that are not easily predictable.

Efficacy limits are another major limitation. The parasitic weed review states that parasitic weed control is challenging because there are few sources of crop resistance and it is difficult to apply controlling methods selective enough to kill the weeds without damaging the crop [N4-F2]. It also notes that parasitic weeds are particularly noxious because they directly extract water and nutrients from the host plant, and that parasitic weeds such as Striga, Orobanche/Phelipanche, and Cuscuta are now threatening food security [N4-F2]. The herbicide evidence adds that the efficacy of each herbicide varies with the parasitic weed species [N4-R1], reinforcing the point that herbicides may work on some species but not others. The same source also states that mechanical weeding and herbicide application are frequently ineffective when applied to parasitic weeds [N4-R3], which means herbicides alone may not be sufficient.

The interaction between crop resistance and weed biology is especially important. The parasitic weed review highlights that parasitic weeds are difficult to control because there are few sources of crop resistance [N4-F2]. The herbicide-treated crop evidence notes that parasitic weed control by introducing resistance to commercial herbicides into crop plants is a current strategy [N4-F2], but the same source emphasizes that controlling parasitic weeds is still difficult because of the need for selective methods that do not damage the crop [N4-F2]. Overall, herbicide-treated crops with target-site resistance offer a partial tool for managing parasitic weeds in legumes, but they are not a silver bullet. It also notes that NTSR involves enhanced metabolism, reduced uptake and translocation, vacuolar sequestration, and increased ability to deal with oxygen radicals [N1-F1]. Because these mechanisms are not limited to target-site changes, resistance traits may be context-dependent and difficult to stabilize. The parasitic weed evidence further emphasizes that parasitic weeds are highly fecund and can rapidly respond to changes in agricultural practices, allowing them to adapt to new hosts and manifest increased aggressiveness against new resistant cultivars [N4-F2]. This suggests that parasitic weed resistance may not only evolve through direct herbicide exposure but may also become more aggressive and persistent over time.

## 2) Operational and agronomic limitations in legumes

Legumes face particular agronomic challenges in parasitic weed management because parasitic weeds are not ordinary weeds. They are described as parasitic plants that rely on neighboring host plants to complete their life cycle and directly extract water and nutrients from the host plant [N4-F2]. This makes them especially damaging once they become established, because they form vascular connections with the host, weaken the crop, and reduce both yield and crop quality [N4-F2].

A major operational limitation is that parasitic weeds are difficult to control with selective methods that do not damage the crop to which they are physically and biochemically attached [N4-F2]. The same source states that parasitic weed control by introducing resistance to commercial herbicides into crop plants is a current strategy, but that controlling parasitic weeds is still challenging [N4-F2]. This implies that herbicide-treated crops may help, but they are not a complete solution. The herbicide evidence also reports that the efficacy of each herbicide varies with the parasitic weed species [N4-R1], meaning that a single herbicide may not work equally well against all parasitic weed species. This variability reduces the practical effectiveness of herbicide-treated crops in legumes.

Another agronomic constraint is herbicide application windows and crop safety. The parasitic weed review notes that parasitic weeds are difficult to apply controlling methods selective enough to kill the weeds without damaging the crop [N4-F2]. This supports the concern that herbicide application must be carefully timed, and that the crop’s physiology and weed competition dynamics make timing especially critical. The evidence also states that parasitic weeds are often difficult to control with mechanical weeding and herbicide application, and that parasitic weeds can persist and cause tremendous yield losses [N4-R3]. Together, these points show that herbicide-treated crops must be used within narrow application windows, and that crop safety remains a major concern.

Finally, effectiveness against diverse parasitic weed species is limited. Legumes are threatened by a range of parasitic weeds, including root feeders, shoot feeders, and species such as Striga, Orobanche/Phelipanche, and Cuscuta [N4-F2]. The review also states that parasitic weed control is challenging because there are few sources of crop resistance and it is difficult to apply selective controlling methods [N4-F2]. This means that herbicide-treated crops may need tailored programs for different parasitic weed species, rather than a single uniform treatment.

## 3) Parasitic weed-specific resistance and management challenges

Parasitic weeds develop herbicide resistance through biological and environmental pathways that are closely tied to their life history. The evidence shows that parasitic weeds are highly fecund, have persistent seedbanks, and respond rapidly to changes in agricultural practices, allowing them to adapt to new hosts and become more aggressive against new resistant cultivars [N4-F2]. This adaptability makes parasitic weed resistance difficult to manage, even when herbicides are used against them.

The branch report on parasitic weed-specific resistance also notes that herbicides may lead to the development of herbicide resistance in parasitic weeds [N6-R2]. Combined with the broader herbicide resistance review, this supports the conclusion that repeated herbicide use can drive resistance evolution in parasitic weeds, and that multiple herbicide resistances are increasingly common [N1-F1]. The review further states that non-target-site resistance is more complicated and trickier to understand than target-site resistance [N1-F1], which implies that parasitic weed resistance may involve multiple pathways that are not easily predictable.

Efficacy limits are another major limitation. The parasitic weed review states that parasitic weed control is challenging because there are few sources of crop resistance and it is difficult to apply controlling methods selective enough to kill the weeds without damaging the crop [N4-F2]. It also notes that parasitic weeds are particularly noxious because they directly extract water and nutrients from the host plant, and that parasitic weeds such as Striga, Orobanche/Phelipanche, and Cuscuta are now threatening food security [N4-F2]. The herbicide evidence adds that the efficacy of each herbicide varies with the parasitic weed species [N4-R1], reinforcing the point that herbicides may work on some species but not others. The same source also states that mechanical weeding and herbicide application are frequently ineffective when applied to parasitic weeds [N4-R3], which means herbicides alone may not be sufficient.

The interaction between crop resistance and weed biology is especially important. The parasitic weed review highlights that parasitic weeds are difficult to control because there are few sources of crop resistance [N4-F2]. The herbicide-treated crop evidence notes that parasitic weed control by introducing resistance to commercial herbicides into crop plants is a current strategy [N4-F2], but the same source emphasizes that controlling parasitic weeds is still difficult because of the need for selective methods that do not damage the crop [N4-F2]. This creates a tension: crop resistance can help suppress parasitic weeds, but parasitic weeds can also evolve resistance to herbicides and adapt rapidly to new hosts and resistant cultivars [N4-F2][N6-R2]. The evidence further states that parasitic weeds are difficult to apply controlling methods selective enough to kill the weeds without damaging the crop to which they are physically and biochemically attached [N4-F2], indicating that even when herbicides are effective, they may still be hard to apply safely in legumes.

## 4) Socioeconomic and ecological limitations

Socioeconomic and ecological limitations are equally important. The evidence indicates that parasitic weeds are a major constraint on agricultural production and that current management methods are limited [N2-R4]. It also states that parasitic weeds are difficult to control with selective methods and that parasitic weeds pose a tremendous threat to world agriculture, often described as “almost uncontrollable” [N2-R5]. This suggests that reliance on herbicides may be only a partial solution, with persistent socioeconomic and ecological trade-offs.

Cost, labor, and farmer adoption barriers are central. The parasitic weed management review notes that the only methods currently available to farmers are resistant varieties and chemical control, although both have their limitations [N2-R4]. It also states that parasitic weeds are difficult to apply controlling methods selective enough to kill the weeds without damaging the crop, which implies that herbicide-based systems may require specialized application equipment, timing, and labor [N4-F2]. The herbicide environmental review adds that herbicides are major elements of plant production and indispensable to modern agriculture, but their influence on the natural environment needs continuous control [N5-F3]. This implies that herbicide adoption may be expensive and labor-intensive, especially in smallholder or resource-constrained settings where farmers face limited access to inputs and mechanization.

Environmental risks and non-target effects are another major limitation. The herbicide environmental review reports that herbicides are usually mixtures of various active substances, making their environmental impact difficult to analyze, and that uncontrolled use has led to adverse effects on non-target organisms [N5-F3]. It also states that herbicides can leach into soil and water systems, cause widespread contamination, and may accumulate in ecosystems, diminishing food safety and posing risks to human health [N5-F3]. The same source notes that herbicides may affect aquatic, soil, and air ecosystems, and that their migration across the environment depends on physicochemical properties such as solubility, partition coefficients, and half-life [N5-F3]. These points support the ecological concern that herbicide-treated crops for parasitic weed control may harm non-target plants, microbes, soil life, and water systems, which is especially problematic in legumes where the crop-weed relationship is already tightly integrated [N5-F3][N4-F2].

Long-term sustainability and resistance management are also critical. The herbicide resistance review explains that repeated use of similar herbicidal modes of action creates selection pressure and leads to the evolution of herbicide resistance in weeds [N1-F1]. It also notes that multiple herbicide resistances are increasingly common, and that non-target-site resistance is more complicated and trickier to understand than target-site resistance [N1-F1]. The parasitic weed evidence adds that parasitic weeds may develop herbicide resistance and that the use of herbicides may lead to the development of herbicide resistances [N6-R2]. This means that herbicide-treated crops with target-site resistance may not be a durable solution, because parasitic weeds can evolve resistance over time, and the same herbicide may become less effective as resistance spreads [N1-F1][N6-R2]. The parasitic weed review also highlights that parasitic weeds are highly fecund and can rapidly respond to changes in agricultural practices, allowing them to adapt to new hosts and manifest increased aggressiveness against new resistant cultivars [N4-F2]. This further undermines long-term sustainability.

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the evidence shows that using herbicide-treated crops with target-site resistance to manage parasitic weeds in legumes is limited by several interrelated factors. Biologically, target-site resistance is specific to herbicides with the same mode of action and does not automatically translate to parasitic weed resistance [N1-R5]. Cross-resistance pathways are plausible under repeated herbicide use, but the evidence does not provide a direct pathway showing how parasitic weeds inherit target-site resistance from crop resistance genes [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Genetically and phenotypically, resistance traits may be unstable or context-dependent, especially when parasitic weeds evolve through non-target-site mechanisms [N1-F1].

Operationally, legumes are constrained by crop physiology and weed competition dynamics because parasitic weeds attach to the host, establish vascular links, and weaken the crop throughout the growing season [N4-F2]. Herbicide application windows must be narrow, and crop safety remains a concern because parasitic weeds are physically and biochemically attached to the host [N4-F2]. Effectiveness against diverse parasitic weed species is also limited, because efficacy varies by species and parasitic weeds can persist and adapt rapidly [N4-R1][N4-F2].

For parasitic weeds specifically, resistance can develop under herbicide pressure, and parasitic weeds are highly fecund, persistent, and adaptable, which makes resistance management difficult [N4-F2][N6-R2]. Efficacy limits are real: parasitic weeds are difficult to control with selective methods, and mechanical weeding and herbicide application are often ineffective [N4-R3]. The interaction between crop resistance and weed biology is therefore both promising and precarious: crop resistance can help, but parasitic weeds can also evolve resistance and become more aggressive against new resistant cultivars [N4-F2][N6-R2].

Socioeconomically and ecologically, the approach faces high cost and labor demands, farmer adoption barriers, environmental contamination, and non-target effects [N2-R4][N5-F3]. Long-term sustainability is threatened by the evolution of herbicide resistance, multiple herbicide resistances, and the difficulty of managing parasitic weeds across changing agricultural practices [N1-F1][N6-R2].

## Final assessment

Overall, herbicide-treated crops with target-site resistance offer a partial tool for managing parasitic weeds in legumes, but they are not a silver bullet. The most important conclusion is that parasitic weeds are especially difficult to control because they are physiological parasites with complex life cycles, rapid adaptation, and persistent seedbanks [N4-F2]. Herbicide-treated crops may reduce parasitic weed pressure in the short term, but they are limited by the biology of the weeds, the specificity of target-site resistance, the complexity of resistance evolution, and the broader ecological and socioeconomic costs of herbicide use [N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R2]. In legumes, where crop physiology and weed competition are tightly coupled, these limitations are especially pronounced.
